TODDLER 3 · LESSON 9

Colors and Shapes for 2-Year-Olds

Age 2 YearsSubject Think & TalkClass Toddler 3Duration 3–5 minutes

At two, everyday life becomes a classroom: the red cup, the round plate, the square window. This class explores eight colors and seven shapes through a short sequence your toddler can join in — look at the cards together, play a few big-button find-it games, match a pair, then take the learning off screen and find colors and shapes around your home.

There is no reading required and nothing to test. You say the words, your toddler taps and points, and every round ends in encouragement, never a score. Short, playful sessions of three to five minutes are all it takes.

Start Today’s Class ↓Look, play, match, then head off screen. Short and playful wins.

SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the colors and shapes pack together.

The printable pack turns this class into eight paper pages: the color cards, the shape cards, two match pages and two hunt pages. Print the pack once and this class keeps working all week — at the table, not on a screen.

  1. 01

    Print the pack

    Open the printable pack and print the eight pages. The card pages love thick paper, but any paper plays.

  2. 02

    Name before cutting

    Cut the color and shape cards out together, naming each one as it is cut — red, circle, blue, square. The cutting is the class.

  3. 03

    Match the pages

    On the match pages, lay each card on its twin and ask “which one goes here?”. One wrong guess is welcome — comparing two things is the thinking work.

  4. 04

    Hunt on paper

    On the hunt pages, circle every red thing, then every circle. A crayon is the right tool, and circling is the right skill.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

Find colors and shapes around you.

The class continues away from the screen. Pick one or two hunts during the day and keep them playful — there is nothing to collect and nothing to prove.

Color hunt

  • Can you find something red?
  • Find something blue.
  • Can you spot something yellow?

Shape hunt

  • Can you find a circle in the room? A plate, a clock or a wheel is a good place to start.
  • Can you find something shaped like a rectangle? Try a book, a door or a box.

Keep hunts short and stay close by. Any noticing counts — naming one red thing together is a complete class.

There is a printable version of these hunts in the Download & Print pack below — handy for the fridge or the weekend.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

Tips for Parents

Sit together in a comfortable spot and let your child hold or tap where they can. Start with the color cards, say each color clearly, and pause — the pause is where your toddler answers in their own way.

Keep the games light. A wrong tap is simply a chance to look together, and every round ends with encouragement rather than a score.

When the on-screen games are done, take the class off screen: hunt for colors and shapes around your home during an everyday moment.

There is no need to finish every section in one sitting, and no need for your toddler to name every color or shape.

Age ranges are a guide. Kiddo School age ranges are guides, not tests or developmental deadlines. Children learn at their own pace.

    Red — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson starts the color deck with the easiest win: red is bright, common and shoutable, and the card-to-room hunt turns one word into a whole-day game.

    What is this?

    Red is a color — the color of fire engines and strawberries — and this card is devoted to it from edge to edge, so nothing competes with the word.

    What does it mean?

    Color words are adjective work: your toddler is learning that red is not a thing but a property of things. That leap starts with one loud, everywhere color.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect wed and red-dy from a two-year-old mouth for months. Say red back clearly once and keep hunting; the mouth catches the ears eventually.

    Why this matters

    Red is usually the first color a two-year-old names, and a first color word opens the door to all the rest. Momentum matters more than accuracy here.

    What it teaches

    Color naming, visual searching, and the first adjective-before-noun habit — red cup, red sock, red everything, happily over-applied.

    Words to learn

    redcolorfindbrightstopstrawberry

    Say this to your child

    “"Red! The whole card is red. Can you spot something red in this room? Look — the red cushion! Say it with me: red. One more… find me another red."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say red — twice, with a pointing finger tracing the whole card, because the entire card is red.
    2. Play the red game in one room: find three red things together — a cushion, a book, a sock — saying red at each find.
    3. Take a red thing and put it next to the card: same! Then hold up something blue and let your toddler push it away — not red.
    4. When your toddler says wed, echo red warmly once and move on; the hunt continues either way.
    5. Slip red into the week: a red cup at dinner, red at the traffic light, a red find on every walk until Friday.

    Look closer at the picture

    This card is the red card — one color, filling the whole picture, with the word red on it for toddlers. Ask your child to say the word while touching the color.

    Ask your child

    "What color is this card?" "Can you find something red in the room?" "Is this red or not?" "Where did you spot red today?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Wed!" shouted at anything remotely reddish — that over-application is the milestone, not a mistake. Some toddlers will simply slap the card and grin; a hand on the color counts as an answer.

    Out in the real world

    Traffic lights, post boxes, fire engines and berries keep red in permanent rotation outdoors. Every sighting is a repetition with the world as the second deck.

    Try it together

    Red treasure basket: drop five red objects and five others into a basket, and let your toddler fish out only the red ones. Wrong fish are fine — they get named and thrown back in.

    Understanding check

    Hold the card up and ask what color it is. A red, a wed or a determined point passes. Then place two objects side by side — if the red one gets picked on request, the word is working.

    Parent tips

    One color at a time beats two for the first week; red is the starter because it is everywhere. Say the word before the object — red cup, not cup that is red — word order sticks early.

    Staying safe

    No safety angle here — the only note is practical: keep the hunted objects too big to swallow, because everything found on a color hunt ends up inspected by mouth at two.

    This lesson pairs with the Red flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

    Blue — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes the calmest color in the deck and gives it two homes: the enormous one overhead and the small ones in the sock drawer.

    What is this?

    Blue is a color — the color of sky and sea — and this card is all blue, so the word and the color arrive together with no rival in sight.

    What does it mean?

    Blue and purple spend months swapping places at two. That confusion is normal sorting work, and side-by-side comparison settles it faster than any explanation.

    What does the child need to know?

    Look up first: the sky is the biggest blue object your toddler will ever own. Then shrink the word down to socks and cups indoors — same word, two scales.

    Why this matters

    Blue is everywhere once you start looking, which makes it the second-easiest color after red. Two colors in hand, the deck starts to feel like a game.

    What it teaches

    Color naming at two scales (vast sky, small sock), visual discrimination between near neighbors, and outdoor-to-indoor word transfer.

    Words to learn

    blueskyseafindcalmcold

    Say this to your child

    “"Blue! Look up — the sky is blue today. Can you find something blue in this room? A blue cup! Say it with me: blue. Blue like the sky, blue like the sea."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say blue, then lift the card towards the ceiling: the sky is blue too, high, high up.
    2. Hunt blue indoors — two finds is a complete round: a blue cup, a blue book, a blue mitten if you own one.
    3. Put the blue card and the purple card side by side and let your toddler compare; eyes sort faster than explanations.
    4. When blue and purple swap places in their speech, say the right word once as you point — no quiz, no correction, just the model.
    5. Make blue a daily check: sky report at the window each morning, one blue find at breakfast, blue pyjamas at night if the drawer cooperates.

    Look closer at the picture

    This card is the blue card — one color from edge to edge, with the word blue printed for toddlers. Ask your child to touch the color and say the word with you.

    Ask your child

    "What color is the sky?" "Can you find something blue in the room?" "Which card is the blue one?" "Is this blue or purple?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Boo!" or "bue!" aimed first at the sky, then at everything below it. Some toddlers will report every cloud as not-blue — that is comparing, and comparing is the lesson.

    Out in the real world

    The morning sky is the free daily repetition; puddles, cars and jeans keep the indoors stocked. Blue is the color your toddler will spot before you do within the week.

    Try it together

    Sky report: a two-second weather check at the window every morning — is the sky blue today? A thumbs-up and the word blue is the whole ritual, and it runs on nothing.

    Understanding check

    Ask what color the card is, then look up together and ask about the sky. Two blues — card and sky — is a full pass. Add a sock-hunt point for extra credit.

    Parent tips

    Keep blue and purple cards neighbours in the deck for a fortnight; the pair teaches each other by proximity. Saying blue before the noun — blue cup — quietly installs word order for free.

    Staying safe

    Nothing risky about color hunting — the one real rule is outdoor edition: when the game happens at a road on the walk, the spotting stops and the hand-holding starts.

    This lesson pairs with the Blue flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

    Yellow — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson puts yellow where it teaches best: on the table. Banana, sweetcorn, egg yolk — snack time is the fastest color classroom in the house.

    What is this?

    Yellow is a color — the color of sunshine and bananas — and this card carries it alone, bright from edge to edge.

    What does it mean?

    Two beats make the word bounce — yeh-low — and lellow is a normal, useful first draft. Keep the bounce; the consonants will land on their own.

    What does the child need to know?

    Food teaches colors faster than anything printed: hold up the banana, say the word, take the bite. Three repetitions at snack time outperform ten at the table with cards.

    Why this matters

    Yellow hides in plain sight all day — ducks, sun, cheese, trucks. A color with a food anchor gets a guaranteed daily rehearsal slot.

    What it teaches

    Color naming through taste and smell (multisensory beats visual alone), two-syllable word practice, and noticing-brightness language.

    Words to learn

    yellowsunbananabrightducksnack

    Say this to your child

    “"Yellow! Bright yellow, like the sun. Look — a banana! Is it yellow? Yes! Can you say yellow? Yeh-low. What else can we find that is yellow?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say yellow — then hold up a real banana beside it: same color, one word.
    2. Run a snack-time yellow hunt: banana, sweetcorn, a square of cheese. Name the color as each one lands on the plate.
    3. Hunt yellow around the house afterwards — the duck in the bath, a yellow toy, a flower on the walk.
    4. When lellow arrives, echo yellow clearly once and hand over the banana; the correction is your pronunciation, never their feelings.
    5. Keep one yellow food in the snack rotation all week so the word has a standing appointment every day.

    Look closer at the picture

    Yellow owns this card from edge to edge, with the word yellow printed underneath. Ask your child to say the word while laying a hand flat on the color.

    Ask your child

    "What color is this card?" "What color is your banana?" "Can you find something yellow in the bath?" "Is the sun yellow?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Lellow!" with a banana held aloft, or a pointing finger at every duck within range. Expect the bath to become a yellow classroom for a week — rubber ducks are enthusiastic assistants.

    Out in the real world

    Bananas, corn on the cob, dandelions, school buses and the sun itself — yellow keeps appointments all day. The food version has the advantage of being eatable.

    Try it together

    Sunshine picnic: lay a yellow cloth or tea towel on the floor and fill it only with yellow snacks and toys. Everything on the blanket must earn its place by being yellow.

    Understanding check

    Ask what color the card is, then what color the banana is. Two yellows — or two lellows — passes completely. A spontaneous yellow! at the fruit bowl ends the assessment early.

    Parent tips

    Snack-time teaching beats table teaching every time at two — appetite opens ears. Keep saying the full word even when lellow is adorable; the two-beat bounce is what they are practising.

    Staying safe

    Food-based color play needs the usual kitchen care: sit down for eating, cut rounds small, and keep the hunt away from the hot stove and the kettle.

    This lesson pairs with the Yellow flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

    Green — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes green outside where it lives: a card in one hand, a leaf in the other, and a walk that becomes a hunt with no preparation at all.

    What is this?

    Green is a color — the color of grass and leaves — and this card is green throughout, ready to be matched to the first plant you meet.

    What does it mean?

    Green is the color toddlers over-use first, calling every plant green including the brown ones. Over-use is a sign the word is being tested — keep it warm and let the sorting come.

    What does the child need to know?

    A hand resting on the grass while the word is spoken teaches more than any picture can. Palm memory is real memory at two.

    Why this matters

    Green has the biggest outdoor territory of any color, so the walk to the shop becomes ten free lessons. No card travels better than this one.

    What it teaches

    Color naming with a touch anchor, nature vocabulary growing alongside (grass, leaf, tree), and over-generalisation — the healthy middle step of all category learning.

    Words to learn

    greengrassleaftreeoutsidegrow

    Say this to your child

    “"Green! Green like grass. Can you touch the grass? Soft — and green. Say green while your hand is on it. Look, a leaf! Green too. How many greens did we find?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say green, then press your palm flat on the card and lift it: we are taking this color outside.
    2. On the walk, stop at the first grass or leaf, put your toddler’s hand on it, and say green while the hand is touching.
    3. Collect the walk’s greens on your fingers — one green for grass, one for a leaf, one for a hedge — and count them on the way home.
    4. When green gets applied to every plant and a few fences, agree warmly and move on: the over-use phase is doing its job.
    5. Bring one green find home — a leaf — and lay it on the card for the match.

    Look closer at the picture

    Green covers this card completely, and the word green sits printed on it. Match it to the first green thing your toddler touches today.

    Ask your child

    "What color is the grass?" "What color is this card?" "Can you find a green leaf?" "How many green things did we see on our walk?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Green!" delivered from the shoulder-height of a pointing arm at grass, trees, hedges and one suspicious bin. Over-use is the sound of a word being tested in the field.

    Out in the real world

    Parks, gardens, weeds in pavement cracks — green is the most available color in any neighbourhood. The walk home is the lesson; the card just names what the fingers find.

    Try it together

    Green gathering walk: collect only green treasures — leaves, fallen needles, one dandelion — into a small bag, then sort the haul onto the green card when you get home.

    Understanding check

    Ask what color the card is and what color the grass is. Two greens passes. The stronger pass is the walk itself: a hand reaching for a leaf while saying the word unprompted.

    Parent tips

    Take the card outdoors at least once — the match between card and leaf is the click. Keep counting the finds; green hunts are the gentlest counting practice in the deck.

    Staying safe

    Outdoor color hunting has one rule worth rehearsing: look with eyes, touch with one gentle hand, and never put leaves, berries or soil anywhere near a mouth.

    This lesson pairs with the Green flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

    Orange — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson doubles up on the deck’s cleverest word: the fruit and the color share one name, so every orange you peel teaches the color three times for free.

    What is this?

    Orange is a color — and also a fruit, which is the rare case where the thing and its color share a name. The card is orange through and through.

    What does it mean?

    One word covering fruit, juice and color is a first homonym: your toddler is learning that words can stretch across meanings. That flexibility starts here.

    What does the child need to know?

    Peel one together, naming the color at the first tear, halfway down and at the first segment — the citrus smell glues the word in place. Carrots and road cones come free afterwards.

    Why this matters

    Orange is scarce in most homes, and scarcity is a game: the hunt for three orange things becomes a proper expedition, and expeditions make words stick.

    What it teaches

    Word-stretching across meanings, smell-assisted memory, and visual searching with a rare target — harder hunting builds better looking.

    Words to learn

    orangepeelfruitjuicesmellsweet

    Say this to your child

    “"Orange! The fruit is orange and the color is orange — same word! Can you smell it? Now we peel… orange, still orange… and a piece for you. Sweet and orange."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say orange, then put a real orange on top of it: the fruit and the color have the same name.
    2. Peel it together, saying orange at the first tear, halfway down, and at the first segment — three names per orange.
    3. Send the family hunting: one orange thing from each room. Scarce is fine — scarce is the game.
    4. When your toddler says oange or just points at the peel, model the word once and hand over a segment.
    5. Keep the streak alive all week: orange juice at breakfast, a carrot at lunch, the orange card wherever the hunt left it.

    Look closer at the picture

    This card is the orange card — one warm color filling the picture, with the word orange printed for toddlers. Ask your child to hold the real fruit against it for the match.

    Ask your child

    "What color is this card?" "What do we call the fruit?" "Can you find something orange in the kitchen?" "What does the orange smell like?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Oange!" with a segment in each fist, or the word saved exclusively for fruit at first and stretched to objects later. The stretch, when it comes, is the milestone.

    Out in the real world

    Oranges, carrots, pumpkins and traffic cones keep the word in circulation. Juice at breakfast is the standing rehearsal; the peel is the classroom.

    Try it together

    Peel-and-match: every peel session ends with one piece of peel laid on the orange card. By Friday the card has a little sculpture, and the word has had a week of rehearsals.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the card is and what the fruit is. If both answers are orange, the homonym has landed. A sniff-and-name at the next orange closes the case.

    Parent tips

    Name the color during the peel, not after — smell and effort glue the word in place. Do not rush the stretching from fruit to objects; one week of fruit-only is a fine pace.

    Staying safe

    Peeling is grown-up hands and little-eyes only — the knife stays away from the table, and pith-covered segments get a quick check for strings before small mouths try them.

    This lesson pairs with the Orange flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

    Purple — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes on the deck’s mouthful: purple, two syllables of genuine difficulty, taught slowly, hunted patiently and applauded in every draft.

    What is this?

    Purple is a color — the color of grapes and lavender — and this card holds it alone, from edge to edge, ready for the hunt.

    What does it mean?

    Purple asks for three consonants in a row, which is why per-per and burple are standard first drafts. Two syllables, one pointed finger, all the time in the world.

    What does the child need to know?

    Purple is scarce in most houses, and that is the game: colour a picture with only the purple crayon, or find one purple thing per room and celebrate each find.

    Why this matters

    The hard words need the gentlest teaching. Purple succeeds when the pressure stays low and the repeats stay high — say it slowly, play it often, accept every draft.

    What it teaches

    Tricky-word articulation, scarcity hunting (looking harder when the target is rare), and the blue-purple near-neighbor sorting that sharpens all color vision talk.

    Words to learn

    purplegrapeslowfindcrayonspecial

    Say this to your child

    “"Purple! Can you say it slowly? Pur… ple. Nice and slow. Look — grapes are purple! Can you find one purple thing in this room? One is plenty. Per-per… purple!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say purple slowly — pur-ple — then again at normal speed, so both versions are on the table.
    2. Hunt purple one room at a time: a book cover, a flower, a sock. If the house runs dry, bring out the purple crayon and colour the hunt instead.
    3. Park the purple card next to the blue card and compare out loud — two nearly-friends, side by side.
    4. When per-per arrives, echo purple slowly once and keep playing; the draft counts, and the polish comes free with repetition.
    5. Feed the word through the week: grapes at snack, a lavender sniff on the walk, purple find number three whenever it turns up.

    Look closer at the picture

    The purple card carries one color and one word, both filling the picture. Say the word slowly together while a finger rests on the color.

    Ask your child

    "What color is this card?" "Can you say purple slowly?" "Can you find something purple?" "Are the grapes purple or green?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Per-per!" or "burple!" — both drafts are welcome and both are on schedule. Some toddlers will skip the word and simply match the crayon to the card; matching is proof enough.

    Out in the real world

    Grapes, lavender, figs and birthday wrapping keep purple in small but steady supply. The garden lavender patch, if you have one, is the card’s outdoor office.

    Try it together

    Purple crayon day: one picture, one crayon, nothing but purple on the page. The scarcity makes the color the whole event, and the word gets said with every stroke.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the card is, slowly. A purple, per-per or burple passes. Then hold up blue and purple together — a correct point at purple on request is the pass with honours.

    Parent tips

    Say it slowly yourself first — your pacing is the model. Never drill the draft away; the word polishes itself through weeks of hearing the full version said warmly.

    Staying safe

    No hazards here — one practical note: grapes at snack time get cut in half lengthways for two-year-olds, and the purple lesson proceeds better with everyone breathing easily.

    This lesson pairs with the Purple flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

    Pink — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson makes pink in front of your toddler: a drop of red into something white — and the mix becomes the memory that separates pink from red for good.

    What is this?

    Pink is a color — the light one, close to red but paler — and this card is pink from edge to edge, with the word printed for toddlers.

    What does it mean?

    Calling pink red is genuinely clever, not wrong: pink is a kind of light red. Agree with the idea, then add the second word — that is how two colors grow from one.

    What does the child need to know?

    The real mix teaches it best: a drop of red juice or paint into something white turns pink before your toddler’s eyes. Watching the color be born beats any explanation.

    Why this matters

    Pink and red live side by side in the deck for a reason — close pairs taught together are what build sharp color vision and sharper sorting talk.

    What it teaches

    Contrast learning inside a color family, cause-and-effect watching (the mix), and the first experience of colours having relatives.

    Words to learn

    pinklightmixredwhitesoft

    Say this to your child

    “"Pink! Soft pink, like the piglet. Watch — a drop of red into the white… stir, stir… PINK! It turned pink! Can you say pink? Pink, red’s gentle sister."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say pink, then hold it next to the red card: sisters — one loud, one soft.
    2. Do the real mix: one drop of red — paint or juice — into something white, stirred by your toddler, watched closely. Pink appears — name it the second it does.
    3. Hunt pink around the house: a blanket, a bottle, a biscuit at snack time. Two finds is a full round.
    4. When pink gets called red, agree and extend: "red like the fire truck — and this one is pink, red’s little sister."
    5. Keep the pair visible all week — both cards on the shelf together — and let the soft one catch up.

    Look closer at the picture

    This card holds one pale color and the word pink. Hold it next to the red card and let your child study the difference out loud.

    Ask your child

    "What color is this card?" "Is pink dark or light?" "What happened when we mixed the colors?" "Can you find something pink in the room?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Pink!" with the mixing spoon still in hand, or a thoughtful pause and then red — followed by your gentle upgrade. The pause-and-correct moment is the lesson happening live.

    Out in the real world

    Piglets at the farm, strawberry ice cream, blossom in spring and one useful biscuit — pink visits often enough. The mix experiment is the anchor memory to revisit.

    Try it together

    Color kitchen: two cups of water, a drop of red in one, and a stir with your toddler commanding the spoon. Add white paint for the full transformation and repeat on demand.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the card is and what the mix made. Two pinks passes. The deeper pass: next time pink is called red, your toddler waits — and self-corrects to pink before you speak.

    Parent tips

    Never overrule red with a no — agree, then add: red’s little sister, pink. Children accept additions far more easily than corrections, and the family metaphor does real work.

    Staying safe

    Paint-and-juice mixing means smocks and wiped surfaces — and anything involving real paint stays taste-safe and out of the mouth, which at two is the actual experiment everyone runs.

    This lesson pairs with the Pink flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

    Black — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson chases the boldest color in the deck: black on the shoes, black on the cat, black on the tyres — with a two-word phrase hiding in the game.

    What is this?

    Black is a color — the darkest one — and this card is black throughout, the highest-contrast target in the whole deck.

    What does it mean?

    Black cat tends to be a toddler’s first two-word phrase: two words, one animal, said at full gallop. Phrases grow out of hunts, and this color hunts well.

    What does the child need to know?

    Start looking and black turns up everywhere — shoes, coat buttons, the letterbox, every tyre on the street. The front-door dash is the fastest hunt in the house.

    Why this matters

    High contrast makes black the easiest color for toddler eyes to spot, which builds the confidence needed for the trickier colors waiting later in the deck.

    What it teaches

    Color naming on a high-contrast target, two-word phrase building, and noticing-the-dark language that later helps with night-and-day talk.

    Words to learn

    blackdarkcattyrenightshoes

    Say this to your child

    “"Black! Look — your shoes are black! My coat has black buttons. Out on the street, the wheels are black — all of them. And is that a black cat? Say it with me: black cat!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say black, then point at your own shoes and the door mat — black lives right by the exit.
    2. Run the doorway hunt: coat buttons, shoes, the letterbox, the bin. Three finds and the round is won.
    3. Take it to the street: every tyre is black, every parked cat might be. Say the pair out loud when one appears: black cat.
    4. When your toddler shouts back for dark brown or dark blue, accept the attempt and point once more — this one here is black, the card’s color.
    5. Keep black on the morning agenda: shoes on, black named, out the door — the routine does the repeating.

    Look closer at the picture

    Black fills this card wall to wall, the word printed for toddlers. Pair it with the shoes by the door for the day’s first match.

    Ask your child

    "What color is this card?" "What color are your shoes?" "Can you find something black by the door?" "Is the cat black?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Black!" with a pointing finger at tyres, shoes and one hopeful cat. Some toddlers will deliver black cat as one breathless word — the phrase is assembling exactly on time.

    Out in the real world

    Tyres, rails, bins and night skies make black the street’s second language. The walk to the car is a black parade; the card rides along in a pocket.

    Try it together

    Black sock sort: pull the black socks from the laundry pile into their own pile — a five-second chore that is also the whole lesson, performed sitting down.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the card is and what colour the shoes are. Two blacks passes. Then watch the next walk — a pointed tyre with the word attached means the colour left the card.

    Parent tips

    Attach black to the shoes-and-coat routine and it rehearses itself every morning without costing a minute. The phrase black cat is worth waiting for; it arrives on its own schedule.

    Staying safe

    Street-based color hunts happen at hand-holding distance from the kerb — the spotting is yours to do while the walking stays safe, and every cat stays admired, never grabbed.

    This lesson pairs with the Black flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

    Circle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson rolls the first shape into the toddler’s hands: trace it, roll it, find it at the breakfast table — round is the shape their day is already full of.

    What is this?

    A circle is the round shape — no corners, no edges, just one curved line — and this card is devoted to it, with the word printed for toddlers.

    What does it mean?

    Circles are usually the first shape named because round things fill a toddler’s day from the first cup to the last ball. The word rides on things they already hold.

    What does the child need to know?

    The roll test is the shape’s signature: a ball rolls, a box refuses. One demonstration teaches round better than a week of pointing.

    Why this matters

    Shape words are pre-maths, and circle is the gateway shape — traced with a finger now, drawn with a crayon next year, read as a letter much later.

    What it teaches

    Shape recognition, finger-tracing fine motor work, and the first property language — round, no corners — that later separates shapes from each other.

    Words to learn

    circleroundrolltracewheelball

    Say this to your child

    “"Circle! Round and round. Can you trace it with your finger? Slowly… all the way round. Look — the ball rolls! Round things roll. Can you find a circle on the table?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say circle, then trace the round edge with one slow finger — your toddler’s finger will chase yours.
    2. Prove the shape: roll a ball across the rug and let a box sit stubbornly still. Round things roll; that is the test.
    3. Hunt circles round the table — the cup’s rim, a plate, a bowl — tracing each one slowly while saying the word.
    4. When your toddler says-ga or just traces the air, take the trace and model the word once beside it.
    5. Roll one ball a day this week with the word attached, and keep the card where snacks are served for the table hunts.

    Look closer at the picture

    This card is the circle card — one round shape filling the picture, with the word circle printed for toddlers. Ask your child to trace the edge with one slow finger.

    Ask your child

    "What shape is this card?" "Can you trace the circle?" "Does the ball roll?" "Can you find a circle in the kitchen?"

    What your child can say or do

    A tracing finger that goes all the way around, or round! aimed at every plate and clock in the house. Some toddlers will roll anything round to prove the point — hands know shapes first.

    Out in the real world

    Wheels, clocks, plates, buttons and the moon run the circle’s outdoor office. Table hunts need no preparation; the round things are already stacked by the sink.

    Try it together

    Roll-or-no game: two bowls, a pile of household objects, and the big question — roll or no roll? Test each one honestly, and let the surprises (a lemon rolls!) carry the thinking.

    Understanding check

    Ask what shape the card is and whether the ball rolls. A circle plus a roll passes. Then watch breakfast — a finger tracing the cup rim without prompting closes the lesson.

    Parent tips

    Trace before you name and name while you trace — the finger and the word teach together. Keep the roll test honest; hands learn shapes faster than eyes ever will.

    Staying safe

    Table hunts use the unbreakable kit only — silicone, plastic and wood — because round things and tiled floors have exactly one arrangement, and it ends in a sweep.

    This lesson pairs with the Circle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

    Square — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson counts the square into your toddler’s world: four corners, one finger, and the boxy things in every room that were squares all along.

    What is this?

    A square is a shape with four equal sides and four corners — it sits still and does not roll, which is how your toddler’s hands will know it.

    What does it mean?

    Counting corners is the first counting-with-a-purpose most toddlers do: one, two, three, four, and the number belongs to the shape. Two words, one game.

    What does the child need to know?

    The square’s party trick is stillness — it does not roll, unlike its friend the circle. Demonstrate both once and the difference moves into the fingers.

    Why this matters

    Squares are the most-seen shape in any house: windows, cushions, books, crackers. Catching them in the wild turns furniture into flashcards.

    What it teaches

    Counting to four with a target, corner-spotting as visual analysis, and the roll-versus-still property contrast that organises the shape world.

    Words to learn

    squarefourcornerssidesstillwindow

    Say this to your child

    “"Square! One, two, three, four — four corners! Can you count them with me? Push it… it sits still. Squares do not roll. Can you find a square in this room? Count its corners!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say square, then count the corners together with one finger — one, two, three, four.
    2. Trace the sides slowly and count them too: four sides, four corners, the same number twice.
    3. Prove the stillness: roll the ball (it goes) and push the square block (it stays). Squares sit still.
    4. Hunt squares in the room — a window, a cushion, a book cover — counting corners on each find.
    5. Hand out square crackers at snack time and count the corners again, with eating allowed as the final step.

    Look closer at the picture

    This card is the square card — one boxy shape filling the picture, with the word square printed for toddlers. Ask your child to count its corners with one finger.

    Ask your child

    "What shape is this card?" "How many corners does it have?" "Does the square roll?" "Can you find a square window?"

    What your child can say or do

    A solemn corner-count that reaches two, three or the full four — every version counts. Some toddlers will push the block across the rug, watch it stop, and announce still! — property language blooming.

    Out in the real world

    Windows, floor tiles, biscuits, waffle grids and picture frames keep squares in view all day. The cracker version is the only one that disappears at the end.

    Try it together

    Corner count parade: walk the room touching four-cornered things — table, cushion, book — and count to four at each one. Counting rides on the walking, and the room does the supplying.

    Understanding check

    Ask what shape the card is and how many corners it has. A square plus any honest corner-count passes. The push test settles the rest: a still square, named as still, is the full diploma.

    Parent tips

    Count with one slow finger, not a fast hand — slow tracing is what teaches the shape. Keep the roll comparison to one line; the square’s stillness needs the circle as its foil.

    Staying safe

    Corner-counting tours pass real furniture with real corners at toddler-eye height — the counting finger is welcome, the running is not, and the coffee table keeps score.

    This lesson pairs with the Square flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

    Triangle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson puts the triangle where toddlers meet it daily: on roofs, on pizza, and cut into the lunch sandwich — three corners, counted slowly, then eaten.

    What is this?

    A triangle is a shape with three sides and three pointy corners — the tent of the shape world, and the roofline of every house drawing ever made.

    What does it mean?

    Three is the new number here: the triangle owns it. Corner-counting to three is a shorter, earlier win than the square’s four, and both grow from the same finger habit.

    What does the child need to know?

    Sandwiches cut corner-to-corner make two instant triangles — the shape arrives at lunch without a single minute of table time. Roofs and pizza slices supply the rest.

    Why this matters

    The triangle gives your toddler the vocabulary of rooftops and mountains, and it is the shape they will most want to draw first — enthusiasm is half the lesson.

    What it teaches

    Counting to three with a visible target, pointy-versus-round property talk, and pre-drawing shape knowledge that pays out at the crayon stage.

    Words to learn

    trianglethreepointyroofcornerslice

    Say this to your child

    “"Triangle! One, two, three — three corners, all pointy. Can you count them? Look up — the roof is a triangle! And your sandwich… two triangles! Count the corners, then eat."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say triangle, then count the corners with one finger — one, two, three. Pointy!
    2. Slice the lunch sandwich corner to corner and count the fresh triangles’ corners before the first bite. Eating the evidence is allowed.
    3. Prove the point: lay a ball and a triangle block on the table and ask which one has the sharp bit. Gentle finger, honest answer.
    4. Hunt triangles out on the walk — roofs, road signs, garden fences — counting to three at each sighting.
    5. Draw one together at the end of the week: wobbly lines count, and the result goes on the fridge as the shape’s portrait.

    Look closer at the picture

    This card is the triangle card — one three-cornered shape filling the picture, with the word triangle printed for toddlers. Ask your child to count the corners with one finger.

    Ask your child

    "What shape is this card?" "How many corners?" "Is it pointy or round?" "What did we eat that was a triangle?"

    What your child can say or do

    A corner-count to three with a triumphant point, or tree-angle said with total confidence — the long word tries itself. Expect sandwich geometry to become a daily demand.

    Out in the real world

    Roofs, mountains, pizza slices, road signs and sandwich halves keep triangles in stock everywhere. The walk home has at least three; the roofline usually has ten.

    Try it together

    Triangle snack lab: cut toast, cheese and cucumber into triangles and sort them onto the triangle card before eating. The shape becomes the plate, and the plate becomes lunch.

    Understanding check

    Name the shape and count its corners together. A triangle plus a corner-count to three passes. A rooftop pointed out on the walk is the pass beyond the card.

    Parent tips

    Count slowly with the finger parked on each corner — speed hides corners from two-year-old eyes. The sandwich trick is worth the extra cut; food shapes are remembered at bedtime.

    Staying safe

    Scissors and knives stay grown-up hands in the triangle kitchen; the toddler job is corner-counting and eating. Pointy corners get touched gently — one soft finger, no poking.

    This lesson pairs with the Triangle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

    Rectangle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson stretches the square into the rectangle: side by side on the floor, long sides and short, with the front door as the giant example your toddler touches daily.

    What is this?

    A rectangle is a shape with four sides — two long ones and two short ones — like a square that has been gently pulled. The card is one, edge to edge.

    What does it mean?

    Short-short-long-long is the rectangle’s rhythm: the shape teaches comparing lengths before it teaches its name. The comparison is the lesson; the label arrives when ready.

    What does the child need to know?

    Rectangle is a mouthful, and long square is a friendly toddler-sized stand-in that is completely honest. Both get said; nobody is corrected.

    Why this matters

    Doors, tables, books and screens make the rectangle the most-touched shape of the day — the front door alone is a life-sized flashcard opened ten times daily.

    What it teaches

    Length comparison (long and short), side-counting that extends the corner habit, and honest interim vocabulary that keeps the game moving before the word matures.

    Words to learn

    rectanglelongshortdoorsidesstretch

    Say this to your child

    “"Rectangle — a long square! Look: two short sides, two long sides. Can you trace them? Short, short… long, long. Now the door — a giant rectangle! You walk through it every day."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say rectangle — then long square, so both names are on the table from the start.
    2. Lay the square card and the rectangle card side by side and trace both: short-short here, looong there. Say it as a rhythm.
    3. Trace the front door’s frame with your toddler — the giant rectangle they walk through all day, now with a name.
    4. Hunt rectangles in the room: books, table tops, the screen you are not watching. Count four sides at each find, long and short.
    5. Keep the pair of cards together all week; the stretched square teaches the rectangle better than any single card could.

    Look closer at the picture

    This card is the rectangle card — one four-sided shape filling the picture, with the word rectangle printed for toddlers. Ask your child to trace the long side, then the short.

    Ask your child

    "What shape is this card?" "Which sides are long?" "Is a rectangle a stretched square?" "Where is the biggest rectangle in our house?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Long square!" delivered as a complete description — take it as a win, because it is. Some toddlers will pat the front door solemnly on the way past all week; the giant example stuck.

    Out in the real world

    Doors, books, tables, screens, biscuit tins and envelopes — rectangles own the house. The book cover is the pocket-sized version your toddler already handles hourly.

    Try it together

    Long-and-short sorting: lay out crayons, blocks and spoons and sort each row into long things and short things. The rectangle’s secret idea — lengths differ — practised on real objects.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the shape is and what happens if you stretch a square. A rectangle, a long square, or both passes. A traced doorframe on the way out is the pass with honours.

    Parent tips

    Say both names warmly and let long square carry the meaning until rectangle grows in — nobody fails a shape test at two. The rhythm short-short-long-long is worth chanting; rhythm is memory.

    Staying safe

    Doorframe tracing walks your toddler past hinges and edges — fingers trace, shoulders stay clear, and the door stays still while it is being measured by a small hand.

    This lesson pairs with the Rectangle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

    Star — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson hands over the deck’s most magical shape: points to count, a twinkle to perform, and wobbly star drawings that count exactly as much as neat ones.

    What is this?

    A star is the shape with points all the way round — five on this card — straight from the night sky, and the word printed for toddlers underneath.

    What does it mean?

    Counting points on a star is counting with a purpose and a natural stop: the points run out. Purposeful counting like this is where numbers start meaning something.

    What does the child need to know?

    The twinkle is the action version — fingers opening and closing in the air, sparkle included. Action-and-shape pairs stick twice as hard as shapes alone.

    Why this matters

    Stars carry the night sky, the Christmas tree and every reward chart ever printed. The shape comes pre-loaded with excitement, which pays the lesson’s bills.

    What it teaches

    Counting points on a fixed target, finger-and-arm twinkle coordination, and shape-drawing courage — wobbly is welcome, and wobbly is how drawing starts.

    Words to learn

    starpointtwinkleskyshinefive

    Say this to your child

    “"A star! Look at all its points. Can you count them with me? One… two… three… four… five! Now twinkle — fingers open, fingers shut. Twinkle, twinkle, little star!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say star, then count the points with one slow finger — one, two, three, four, five.
    2. Twinkle together: hands up high, fingers opening and shutting, a little twinkle sound included. Sparkle is mandatory.
    3. Hunt stars in books, on clothes, on the reward chart — counting the points at each find, even the four-pointed rebels.
    4. When your toddler’s count reaches three or six, take the count and keep the finger slow; precision arrives with practice, delight arrives now.
    5. Close the week with a star-drawing session — wobbly lines welcome — and tape the results to the window for the sky to see.

    Look closer at the picture

    This card is the star card — one pointed shape filling the picture, with the word star printed for toddlers. Ask your child to count the points with one slow finger.

    Ask your child

    "What shape is this card?" "How many points does the star have?" "Can you twinkle like a star?" "Where do stars live at night?"

    What your child can say or do

    A five-point count that ends wherever it ends, plus hands twinkling above the head at any mention of the word. Expect star! at every ceiling light for a fortnight.

    Out in the real world

    The real sky is the free field trip: on a clear evening, look up together and join the card to the sky with a single sentence. Fairy lights and gift wrap keep the indoor supply going.

    Try it together

    Star factory: fold-none, draw-many — your toddler draws, you cut, and the results get taped to the window. Counting points on their own artwork is the proudest maths there is.

    Understanding check

    Ask what shape the card is and how many points it has. A star plus any honest point-count passes. A spontaneous twinkle at bedtime is the pass with glitter on it.

    Parent tips

    Count the points slowly and stop when they run out — the natural ending is the lesson. Never redraw their stars; wobbly lines are the evidence of a first attempt, and first attempts are the treasure.

    Staying safe

    Star-cutting is grown-up scissors; the toddler runs the drawing and the sticky tape. Window displays go above reaching height, well away from cords and catches.

    This lesson pairs with the Star flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

    Heart — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson teaches the one shape that carries a feeling: trace it, name it, and give it away — because the heart card is really about saying I love you in shape form.

    What is this?

    A heart is the shape with two rounded bumps up top and one point down below — the shape everyone agrees means love, and this card is one, edge to edge.

    What does it mean?

    The heart links a shape to a feeling: a shape word and a feeling word in the same breath. It is the only card in the deck that doubles as a message.

    What does the child need to know?

    Trace it slowly — bump, bump, point — and the shape teaches itself. Drawing one and handing it over as a heart for you is the lesson’s natural ending.

    Why this matters

    Feelings make shapes repeatable — toddlers rehearse whatever feels warm, and this card feels warm every time it comes out. That warmth pays the lesson’s bills.

    What it teaches

    Shape tracing with an emotional anchor, giving-and-receiving language, and the first shape-plus-meaning pairing — the foundation of symbols, years early.

    Words to learn

    heartlovebumpspointtracehug

    Say this to your child

    “"A heart! Bump, bump… and down to the point. Can you trace it? The heart is the shape for love. Here — I drew you a heart. It means I love you. Will you draw one for teddy?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say heart, then trace it slowly with one finger — bump, bump, down to the point.
    2. Trace it on your toddler’s back and let them guess the shape; skin learns shapes surprisingly well.
    3. Say the meaning plainly: the heart is the shape for love. Then draw one and hand it over — a heart for you.
    4. Hunt hearts in books, on cards and on pajamas; every find gets traced with one gentle finger.
    5. Finish the week with a heart-giving round: one drawing for each family member, delivered by the artist in person.

    Look closer at the picture

    This card is the heart card — one shape filling the picture, with the word heart printed for toddlers. Ask your child to trace the two bumps and the point with one finger.

    Ask your child

    "What shape is this card?" "Which way do the bumps go?" "What does the heart shape mean?" "Who should get a heart drawing today?"

    What your child can say or do

    A careful finger tracing the whole shape, or a crumpled heart drawing pressed into your hand with no words at all. Heart! aimed at the pancake on the plate is also correct.

    Out in the real world

    Birthday cards, biscuit cutters, love notes and pancakes keep hearts in rotation. The giving is the everyday version: any drawing becomes a heart when it is handed over with love.

    Try it together

    Heart delivery: draw a batch, cut them out together, and let your toddler deliver one to every family member — teddy included. The delivering is the game; the shape rides along.

    Understanding check

    Ask what shape the card is and what the shape means. A heart plus love passes completely. The deeper pass: a heart given away without being asked — the lesson doing its own work.

    Parent tips

    Say the feeling word every time you say the shape — heart, love — the pair is the whole design. Keep the receiving enthusiastic; a heart accepted with a hug gets repeated forever.

    Staying safe

    Heart-cutting belongs to grown-up scissors, and the tracing finger stays gentle on backs and tummies — skin-tracing is a calm-down game, not a tickle war, and everyone can tell the difference.

    This lesson pairs with the Heart flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

    Oval — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson brings the deck’s sneakiest shape to the breakfast table: a real egg beside the card, one finger tracing the stretch — the oval settles its argument with the circle by itself.

    What is this?

    An oval is an egg of a shape: take one circle and pull it gently longer. The card shows one, plain and simple, with the word printed for toddlers.

    What does it mean?

    Oval against circle is a real puzzle at two, and the breakfast egg settles it more neatly than any explanation: one is egg-shaped, one is round. Hands sort it; words follow.

    What does the child need to know?

    Park a real egg beside the card at breakfast, trace egg then card, and let the two shapes introduce themselves. The wobbly roll is the oval’s signature move.

    Why this matters

    The oval completes the shape family’s gentle ending: after corners and points, a shape that is almost a circle but not quite — the finest distinction in the deck.

    What it teaches

    Fine shape discrimination (almost-round versus round), real-object matching, and the quiet pride of spotting the difference grown-ups gloss over.

    Words to learn

    ovaleggstretchwobblytraceroll

    Say this to your child

    “"Oval! Like an egg. A circle that got stretched — see? Trace it with me, the long way round. Roll it… wobble, wobble! Eggs are ovals. Can you find the egg shape?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say oval, then trace the long way round with one slow finger — a circle, but stretched.
    2. Hold a real egg beside the card at breakfast: same shape. Trace the egg gently, then trace the card.
    3. Compare with the circle card: this one is round, this one is stretched. Lay them side by side and let your toddler point at each on request.
    4. Prove the difference: roll the ball (smooth), roll the egg-shaped object (wobbly). The wobble is the oval’s name in movement.
    5. Hunt ovals through the week — a spoon bowl, a cucumber slice cut lengthways, a balloon — with egg mornings as the anchor.

    Look closer at the picture

    This card is the oval card — one stretched-round shape filling the picture, with the word oval printed for toddlers. Ask your child to trace it the long way with one finger.

    Ask your child

    "What shape is this card?" "What is shaped like an egg?" "Is the oval round like the circle or stretched?" "Which one rolls wobbly?"

    What your child can say or do

    A slow tracing finger that stretches further than it should, or egg! aimed at the breakfast plate — which is the right answer wearing a smaller word. Wobbly-roll experiments will follow.

    Out in the real world

    Eggs, balloons, lemons, plums and spoon bowls carry the oval through the week. Breakfast is the standing appointment; the card lives by the egg cups.

    Try it together

    Wobbly roll derby: an egg-shaped object, a ball, and a short ramp of cushions — which rolls smooth, which wobbles? The oval announces itself in motion, no words required.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the card is and what it looks like. An oval, an egg, or a stretched circle — any of the three passes. A wobbly-roll demonstration on request is the pass with honours.

    Parent tips

    Let the egg do the teaching — real objects beat explanations at two, and breakfast repeats daily. Keep circle and oval cards neighbours; the almost-twins sharpen each other.

    Staying safe

    Eggs at the table sit in egg cups, not on edges — one grab and the lesson becomes a clean-up. Tracing a real egg happens with a gentle finger and a grown-up’s hand underneath.

    This lesson pairs with the Oval flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).
